title: Short-Term Rental Rules in 2026: What's Changing and How It's Enforced | Keegix Podcast
description:
Airbnb's new house rules policy (from Nov 20, 2026), how short-term rental rules are enforced in Nova Scotia, Halifax, Toronto, Ottawa, B.C., Quebec, New York City, Spain and the EU, and the safety basics hosts are expected to cover.
Plus a five-step to-do list for hosts this month.
Hosts and guests on this show are AI voices. Facts are sourced below. Rowan is a fictional AI character, not a real person.
Rules are as of October 2026, vary by city and province, and change. Not legal advice.

lines.text: For Airbnb reservations booked from November twentieth, asking guests to strip the beds or wash the dishes at checkout is generally not allowed. And the listing editor is already flagging it.

And it isn't only the platforms tightening up. In Nova Scotia, running a short term rental without registering can bring fines of up to one hundred thousand dollars for each year. In Toronto, your registration number has to appear on every listing and every ad.

card.label: Max fine per year for an unregistered short-term rental in Nova Scotia

lines.text: So today, we're going through what's changing, how it actually gets enforced, and what to do about it this month.

Welcome to the Keegix Podcast, a weekly show about running a B and B, a cottage, or a short term rental. I'm June, your A I host. Everyone you hear on this show is an A I voice, and the facts we use are sourced in the description.

This is episode one, and we're starting with rules. We'll cover Airbnb's new house rules policy, how cities and provinces in Canada enforce short term rental rules, a few examples from around the world, and the safety basics most hosts are expected to cover. Then we'll finish with a short list of what to do before the end of November.

My guest is Rowan. Rowan is an A I character we built to play a B and B owner with twenty years behind the desk. Not a real person, and not a lawyer. Just a practical voice for the host's side of things. Welcome, Rowan.

card.text: Rowan is an AI character playing a B&B owner. Not a real person.

lines.text: Thanks, June. And I'll say it up front, since we're talking rules all episode. Everything here is as of October twenty twenty six. Rules vary a lot by city and province, and they change. Use this as a map, then check your own city's page.
Good. Let's start with the one most hosts are hearing about right now.

segments.heading: Airbnb's new house rules policy explained

lines.text: Rowan, Airbnb started rolling this out on October twentieth. What actually changes?

The new house rules policy applies to reservations booked on or after November twentieth, twenty twenty six. The big shift is that Airbnb now splits what you tell guests into two buckets. House rules, which guests have to follow. And requests, which guests are encouraged to follow, but which aren't binding.

card.title: Airbnb
card.text: New house rules policy applies to reservations booked on or after Nov 20, 2026.

lines.text: So what counts as a house rule now?

There are seven standard ones. Maximum overnight guests. Quiet hours. Events. Pets, including whether they're allowed and how many. Smoking, which covers vaping and e cigarettes. Commercial photography and filming. And lock up at checkout, with optional details about where to return the keys.

card.label: Standard house rules Airbnb hosts can set, from guest limits to lock-up at checkout

lines.text: That's a short list. Where does everything else go?
Into requests. Those are the things you'd like guests to do during the stay or before they leave. And this is where the checkout chores come in.
Which checkout chores can hosts still ask Airbnb guests to do?

Airbnb's examples of requests that are generally allowed are pretty light. Put used dishes in the sink. Gather used towels. Separate trash and recycling into the bins inside. Turn off the air conditioning when you leave.
And what's not allowed?

Washing and putting away dishes. Stripping the beds or starting laundry. Taking garbage off site. And asking guests not to use an amenity you advertised, like the air conditioning. Airbnb's thinking is simple. If it's a job a cleaner would normally do, it shouldn't land on the guest.
I can hear some hosts groaning. Especially in small places where the host is the cleaner.

I get it. In a small B and B, you are the cleaner. But picture the guest's side. They paid a cleaning fee, then they spend their last hour on your sheets. Airbnb's own explanation is that surprise chores hurt the stay, and they hurt the reviews.
So say your cottage is on a septic system, and you don't want wipes flushed. Is that a rule or a request?

It isn't one of the seven standard rules, so it goes in requests. Write it plainly and say why. Please don't flush wipes, the cottage is on a septic system. Guests follow a request much more often when they understand the reason.
Are there exceptions?

A few, and they're sensible. Airbnb says what's reasonable depends on the listing type, the stay, and local factors. Its examples are limiting shower time during local drought restrictions, and asking guests to use animal proof trash bins in bear country. Those are about the place, not about saving the host some labour.
What about a rule that comes from your condo board or the town? Say, no parking on the street overnight.

Airbnb lets you give notice of local rules that could lead to fines from a homeowners association, building security, or local government. You put that in the designated section of the listing. You're not fining the guest. You're warning them about someone else's rule.
Can a sign by the door still add a new rule for Airbnb guests?

No, and this part catches a lot of hosts. All house rules and requests have to be in the section of the listing called House rules and requests. Airbnb says you can't add new ones later through messages, other parts of the listing, signs in the home, or in person.

card.text: On Airbnb, rules and requests must live in the listing's House rules section.

lines.text: So the laminated sign in the kitchen that says strip the beds before you go.

That sign can't create a new rule. Whatever is on your signs, in your binder, or in your welcome book should match the listing. It can repeat the rules and explain them. It just shouldn't add to them.
That's a good habit anyway. One set of rules, said the same way everywhere.
Exactly. If a guest reads one thing on the listing and something else on the fridge, you've already lost the argument.
That's the policy as of October twenty twenty six. Check Airbnb's help centre for the latest wording before you edit. This isn't legal advice.

segments.heading: How Airbnb enforces house rules, fees and contracts

lines.text: Okay, Rowan. Say a host ignores all this and keeps strip the beds in their requests. What happens?

Airbnb has laid out a ladder. First, the listing editor highlights requests that don't comply. If a host saves it anyway, they get an email with tips, and they can appeal. If it still isn't resolved, guests may see an alert on the listing, something like includes cleaning requests.
That's a pretty public flag.
It is. And for persistent violations, Airbnb says it may post a notice on the listing, reduce the listing's visibility in search, or take other action under its terms of service.

card.title: How Airbnb enforces it
items: Email with a chance to appeal

lines.text: Can an Airbnb host charge a guest for skipping the checkout list?

No. Airbnb's ground rules for guests say cleaning fees cover standard cleaning, and hosts may not charge guests fees for failing to do specific cleaning or checkout tasks. You can still leave an honest review about cleanliness.
And fines in general?

The new policy says hosts can't impose fines or other penalties on guests. It also rules out charging for advertised features that weren't in the price at booking, and restricting access to anything you advertised. Fees for optional extras, like a breakfast service, can be described in your requests.

card.text: No host fines on Airbnb guests. No hidden fees for advertised features.

lines.text: So if a guest actually causes damage?
Talk to the guest, document it, and request reimbursement through Airbnb's Resolution Centre. That's the route Airbnb wants for damage, rather than a fine written into your house rules.
Let's talk paperwork. A lot of hosts send a rental agreement, or ask for a photo of the guest's identification.

Generally, not anymore. Airbnb says hosts may not require separate contracts or ask for personal information like government identification, unless the law requires it or it's one of a few allowed cases. For contracts, those cases include legal requirements, homeowners association rules, monthly stays, Airbnb Luxe listings, and optional amenities, like a golf cart.

card.title: Airbnb contracts
card.text: Separate contracts only for legal or HOA requirements, monthly stays, Luxe, or optional amenities.

lines.text: And if a guest breaks one of the real house rules?

Then you have some backing. Airbnb says a host can cancel without fees or other consequences if a guest breaks a house rule during the stay, or says before check in that they plan to. That's a good reason to put the rules that matter most, like your guest limit, into the standard rules and not just a paragraph of text.
That's the part people miss. The rules you can lean on are the short list.
Short, clear, and in the right box.
Again, this is as of October twenty twenty six, and Airbnb can update these pages. This isn't legal advice.

segments.heading: How Canada enforces short-term rental rules: Nova Scotia, Halifax, Toronto, Ottawa

lines.text: Let's move from the platform to the government. Rowan, when people say a city is cracking down, what does that actually look like?

Most of it comes down to a few tools. A registration number you have to get and show on every listing. A principal residence rule, meaning you can only rent out the home you actually live in. Sometimes a cap on nights. Fines. And more and more, the platforms themselves have to check numbers and take listings down.
Start close to home. Nova Scotia.

Nova Scotia has a provincial registry. If you rent a place for twenty eight days in a row or less, you have to register before you operate. That covers short term rentals and traditional places like B and Bs, cottages, even yurts. Each location needs its own registration number, and you renew every year by April first.
Say someone buys a cottage this fall that the last owner already rented out. Can they keep using that number?

No. The province says a registration can't be transferred to a new owner. The new owner has to register before operating. And the province says to expect two to three weeks to get a number, sometimes longer, so don't leave it until the week before your first booking.
What does it cost?

It depends on the type. A primary residence short term rental is fifty dollars a year. A commercial short term rental is two thousand dollars in the busiest tier, which includes Halifax and Dartmouth, five hundred in most other communities, and two hundred and forty in a handful of smaller towns.

card.label: Nova Scotia's yearly registration fee, by type and location

lines.text: And how is it enforced?

The regulations say any online ad for your place has to include your registration number, and platforms have to make sure postings show a valid one. Platforms also have to remove an ad when the minister asks, and share their records on request. On the penalty side, the province lists fines of up to one hundred thousand dollars for each year a place isn't registered. There are also administrative penalties of two thousand dollars for a first offence, four thousand for a second, and eight thousand after that.

card.title: Nova Scotia
card.text: Online ads must include your registration number. Platforms must remove ads when the minister asks.

lines.text: Halifax adds its own layer, right?

Yes. Since September twenty twenty three, in Halifax's residential zones, short term rentals are only allowed in the owner's primary residence. You can rent out the whole home while you're away, but a basement apartment or a backyard suite has to be rented for more than twenty eight days. Commercial and mixed use zones are different, so check the zoning for your address.
What are Toronto's short term rental rules?

You register with the city, it has to be your principal residence, and since you only have one of those, you can only run one short term rental. If you rent the entire unit, there's a cap of one hundred and eighty nights a year. Renting up to three bedrooms while you live there has no night cap. The registration fee is three hundred and ninety dollars.

card.label: Toronto's yearly cap for renting out an entire unit

lines.text: And the number has to show up everywhere?

On every listing and ad, plus related invoices and receipts. Your listing's name and address must match exactly. Toronto's set fines include one thousand dollars for not registering or advertising an unregistered rental, and seven hundred dollars for going over the night cap. If it goes to court, fines can reach one hundred thousand dollars.
And Ottawa?

Ottawa uses a host permit. You need one to rent your principal residence, or part of it, for fewer than thirty nights in a row. Every listing has to show your permit number and the maximum number of overnight guests, and hosts can only list on platforms that are registered with the city. Rural cottages have their own separate permit.

card.title: Ottawa
card.text: Listings must show the host permit number and maximum overnight guests.

lines.text: All of that is as of October twenty twenty six, and every one of these cities can change its rules. Check your city and province before you list. This isn't legal advice.

segments.heading: BC, Quebec and the world: registration numbers and platform takedowns

lines.text: Now let's look at places where the platform does a lot of the enforcing. British Columbia first.

B C runs a provincial registry. Since May first, twenty twenty five, hosts have had to show their provincial registration number on listings, along with a local business licence number where one is required. The yearly fee is one hundred dollars if you live in the rental, and four hundred and fifty if you don't.
And the principal residence rule?

In some parts of the province, short term rentals are limited to the host's principal residence, plus one secondary suite or accessory dwelling unit on the same property. Other areas don't apply it. The province has a map, so look up your address.
Where do the platforms come in?

This is the strict part. Larger platforms have to validate registration numbers every day through the registry. If a listing fails, the platform has to stop advertising it, block new bookings, and cancel existing ones. Platforms also send monthly data reports, including host names, addresses and booking history, and local governments can get that data for bylaw enforcement.

card.title: British Columbia
card.text: Larger platforms validate registration numbers daily and must remove listings that fail.

lines.text: So nobody has to knock on your door.
Right. The listing just disappears. And if a local government asks for a takedown after giving notice, the platform has five days to act.
Quebec?

Quebec is very specific about display. Every ad has to show the registration number, which is six digits. On a booking platform, the certificate's expiry date has to show too. And the registration certificate itself has to be displayed at the main entrance, where guests can see it.
What are the fines like?

For an individual, leaving the number out of an ad is one thousand to ten thousand dollars. Operating without registration is two thousand five hundred to twenty five thousand. A platform company that publishes a listing without a number faces up to one hundred thousand dollars. Quebec also expects hosts to carry liability insurance of at least two million dollars per event.

card.label: Max fine for a platform company publishing a Quebec listing without a number

lines.text: Let's go global. New York City is the one everyone mentions.

Under New York's Local Law eighteen, hosts register with the city's Office of Special Enforcement. A short term rental is only legal if the host lives in the same unit with the guests, and there's a limit of two guests, not counting children under four. Since September twenty twenty three, booking platforms can't process transactions for unregistered rentals.

card.title: New York City
card.text: Host must live in the unit with guests. Maximum two guests, not counting children under 4.

lines.text: Spain?

Spain built a single national registry. Since July first, twenty twenty five, tourist and seasonal rentals need a registration code to advertise on platforms. In February twenty twenty six, the housing ministry ordered the removal of more than eighty six thousand ads for properties that didn't meet the requirements.

card.label: Rental ads Spain's housing ministry ordered removed, Feb 2026

lines.text: And Barcelona went further.

Barcelona announced in June twenty twenty four that it plans not to renew its roughly ten thousand tourist apartment licences when they come up in November twenty twenty eight. That one is worth watching for updates.
And the European Union?

The European Union's short term rental data regulation started applying on May twentieth, twenty twenty six. It sets common standards for countries that use host registration. Platforms verify registration numbers and send activity data to public authorities every month.

card.text: EU short-term rental data rules apply from 20 May: number checks, monthly data.

lines.text: So the pattern really is the same everywhere.
Get a number, show the number, and expect the platform to check the number. If you host in more than one place, keep one list with every registration and every renewal date.
All as of October twenty twenty six. These rules vary and they change. This isn't legal advice.

segments.heading: Short-term rental safety checklist: alarms, extinguishers, first aid

lines.text: Let's get practical. Safety. What are hosts commonly expected to have?

Start with alarms. Ontario's fire marshal guidance for short term rentals says working smoke alarms and carbon monoxide alarms should be outside each sleeping area and on every storey. Local rules may require more, so check with your fire department.
Does Airbnb require them?

Airbnb strongly urges hosts to have smoke and carbon monoxide alarms, test them regularly, and keep the safety devices section of the listing up to date. If your place only has electric appliances and no attached garage, you can mark that a carbon monoxide alarm isn't needed. Guests see that section, so keep it accurate.
What should be on a short term rental safety checklist, beyond alarms?

A good model is the self check list the District of Squamish in B C gives its short term rental operators. Test smoke and carbon monoxide alarms monthly and keep a log. Replace smoke alarms before they're ten years old. Have a fire extinguisher mounted and serviced every year. Keep a level one first aid kit on hand. And post a fire safety plan near the exits, plus emergency contact information.
Posting emergency information comes up a lot.
It does, and in Toronto it's required. Since June twenty twenty four, operators there have had to post emergency contact information and exit diagrams in the rental.
Does anyone actually come and check?
In Toronto, yes. The city started annual compliance inspections in twenty twenty five, and the operator has to be there.

card.title: Toronto
card.text: Post emergency contact information and exit diagrams inside the rental.

lines.text: What would you put on that emergency page?

The full civic address, because that's what you give emergency services. Your phone number and a backup contact. Where the extinguisher, the first aid kit and the main water shutoff are. And the two ways out of every room, which the Ontario guidance also stresses. Doors and windows to the outside should open easily.
Say a guest arrives late at night at a cottage on a dirt road. What do they need most?

The address, the nearest hospital, and a number that will actually get answered. Put it in two places. On paper by the door, and on whatever they can open on their phone. And one tip for barbecues, since cottages love them. The Squamish list says keep them at least one metre from anything that can burn.
As always, your local fire code decides what's required where you are. This isn't legal advice.

segments.heading: Recap: what hosts should do this month

lines.text: Let's turn all of this into a to do list for the next few weeks. Rowan, number one.
Before November twentieth, open the House rules and requests section of your Airbnb listing. Move your must have rules into the seven standard rules, and cut any chores a cleaner should be doing.

card.title: This month
items: Fix Airbnb house rules by Nov 20

lines.text: Two.
Make your signs, your binder and your welcome book match the listing. They can repeat the rules, but they can't add new ones.
Three.
Find your registration or permit number. Check that it's on every listing and ad, and put the renewal date in your calendar. In Nova Scotia, that's April first.
Four.
Check whether a principal residence rule applies to your address, especially if you rent out a suite or a second property.
And five.
Walk through the place with a safety checklist. Test the alarms, check the extinguisher and the first aid kit, and post the emergency page by the door.

That's episode one of the Keegix Podcast. If you'd like your house rules, checkout list and emergency information in one page guests can open on their phone, you can start free for one property at keegix dot com slash start.
